#614. A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms

A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.

The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.

The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?

Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance

To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.

At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.

The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.

Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.

Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.

A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans

One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.

The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).

This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.

"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."

Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.

Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.

One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.

"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."

There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.

In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.

Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?

The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.

Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.

Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.

For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.

"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

#613. Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking

Alexander Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the No. 1 spot in tennis.

Germany's Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in men's tennis, capping a year in which he won two Grand Slams.

Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.

Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.

Zverev got there by reaching the quarterfinals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.

The 29-year-old is the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe achieved the feat at age 30 in 1974.

"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.

"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."

Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.

Zverev's career had long been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching the pinnacle, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.

But he finally had its broke through this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.

Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.

The Hamburg-born Zverev also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet.

While it did end up flying by Mars, the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars.

When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars.

Ever since Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope to the red-tinted star and identified as a planet, Mars has captivated scientists' interests as to its nature. So it was of no surprise that as soon as we gained the ability to send missions into space, that the focus turned to the "fourth rock from the Sun."

As it turned out, though, reaching Mars, let alone entering its orbit or landing on its surface,, was and continues to be difficult.

Mars 1, despite its name, was actually the Soviet Union's fourth attempt at sending a probe to the planet. The first three ended in launch failures. Similar problems faced the United States, as well, but it was NASA's Mariner IV mission that became the first to successfully fly by Mars two years later.

Still, as humanity continues to push forward to the day people land on, explore and live on Mars, the 1962 Soviet mission stands as the first to get close to revealing the first details about the planet.

#611. The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?

Why did crocodiles survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago? New research suggests that their preference for warm environments may have given them a crucial advantage during one of Earth's greatest mass extinctions.

Scientists led by UCL (University College London) found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250 million years of evolutionary history following warm climates rather than adapting to dramatically different temperatures. When Earth grew hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes reaching as far as Antarctica. As temperatures fell, they moved back toward the tropics.

Published in Science Advances, the study analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. Researchers combined this evidence with computer models that reconstructed Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years.

The results suggest that tropical and subtropical regions remained suitable for crocodile relatives after the asteroid struck, even as the environments available to many dinosaurs deteriorated. Only the most extreme climate simulations eliminated these potential refuges.

Why Crocodiles Survived the Dinosaur Extinction

The researchers examined how conditions on Earth may have changed following the asteroid impact 66 million years ago. Their simulations indicated that areas near the equator could have remained warm enough to support crocodile relatives, providing places where surviving populations could persist and eventually recover.

Previous modeling by members of the same research team found that suitable habitats for non-avian dinosaurs (i.e., the ones that went extinct) contracted much more severely after the impact.

Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group.

"Crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out."

The discovery offers a possible explanation for how a group of animals that appeared around the same time as dinosaurs managed to endure two of Earth's five major mass extinctions.

Modern crocodiles and their close relatives share many recognizable features, but their evolutionary history reveals a much wider variety of body shapes, sizes, and lifestyles.

The broader crocodile lineage, known as pseudosuchians, once included heavily armored plant eaters, predators that hunted entirely on land, and enormous animals weighing more than a metric ton.

Among the most remarkable was Sarcosuchus, a giant predator nicknamed the "super croc" that could reach 12 meters in length. Another prehistoric relative, Postosuchus, was a land dwelling hunter capable of moving on either two legs or all four.

Dr. Chiarenza said: "Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug.

"Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate."

Fossils Reveal 245 Million Years of Climate History

To investigate that relationship, the scientists reconstructed the temperature and rainfall preferences of 400 crocodile species and their ancient relatives. They used fossil evidence, evolutionary family trees, and detailed maps of where living crocodile species are found today.

The team then compared these preferences with reconstructions of ancient geography and climate to identify where suitable habitats existed at different points in Earth's history.

A clear pattern emerged. Crocodile relatives generally followed warmer conditions as the planet's climate changed, expanding their ranges during hot periods and retreating when temperatures cooled.

About 50 million years ago, during the particularly warm early Eocene, global temperatures were approximately 10°C higher than today, and the polar regions had no permanent ice. Crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes across North America, Europe, and even Antarctica.

Over the following millions of years, global cooling gradually reduced the areas where they could thrive. Their geographic range contracted toward warmer tropical regions.

Although this preference for warm environments remained remarkably consistent, the researchers identified two important exceptions.

During the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, approximately 94 million years ago, global temperatures climbed as much as 14°C above modern levels. One branch of the crocodile family tree evolved the ability to tolerate hotter conditions than the broader lineage could withstand at other times.

A separate adaptation occurred around 34 million years ago in Australia. As a prolonged cooling period reduced rainfall and dried out the continent, an extinct group of crocodiles adapted to increasingly arid, desert-like environments.

These exceptions show that some crocodile relatives could evolve to handle different climates, even though most continued to follow their preferred warm conditions.

What Happened After the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid?

The researchers also used climate simulations to investigate the decades and centuries immediately following the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered the extinction of most dinosaurs.

They explored several possible environmental consequences, including sunlight being blocked by dust and ash and rising carbon dioxide levels associated with volcanic eruptions.

When the simulations reduced sunlight by 5% or 10%, warm regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives. These areas could have provided critical refuges during the environmental disruption.

However, a more severe scenario involving a 15% reduction in sunlight left those regions unsuitable as well. The researchers noted that this extreme level of reduced sunlight is now considered unlikely.

Other simulated changes, including increased atmospheric carbon dioxide, did not alter the availability of suitable climates for crocodiles.

Together, the results suggest that crocodiles may have benefited from living in regions where temperatures remained within their preferred range, even as conditions became much less favorable for many dinosaurs.

The Survival Strategy That Could Now Become a Weakness

The researchers emphasized that favorable temperatures were probably only one reason crocodiles survived the mass extinction.

Other characteristics likely improved their chances, including relatively small body sizes, the ability to live partly in water, flexible diets, and modest energy requirements. As ectothermic ("cold-blooded") animals, crocodiles need less food to maintain their bodies than many animals that generate their own body heat.

The findings also raise important questions about how crocodiles will respond to modern climate change.

For millions of years, moving into regions with suitable temperatures appears to have been one of their main responses to a changing planet. Today, however, expanding cities, agricultural land, and roads increasingly limit where wildlife can move.

Professor Philip Mannion, based at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "These findings have implications for species today. If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today's species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder."

The research was funded by The Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust, and the National Environment Research Council (NERC).

"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth. It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina.

That April 1 event — an incoming meteor, also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors.

Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic.

That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

This skyfall show is among a number of recent episodes that spotlight the value of combining multi-sensor data to not only portray fireball dynamics but also to help appreciate human-caused space debris impacts, as well as strengthening planetary defense knowhow.

Take, for instance, another extraterrestrial incident.

In this case, an April 24, 2025 fireball over south-central Alaska yielded one of the most densely recorded "seismoacoustic" datasets ever obtained for a nature-made bolide en route to busting up.

A network of 37 seismic stations, 16 single infrasound sensors, and four infrasound arrays recorded 30 ballistic and multiple fragmentation arrivals. All this was complemented by Doppler weather radar detections of falling meteorites and independent optical video observations.

Now, toss in for good measure yet another encounter.

A roughly 12-foot-wide (3.7 meters) space rock plowed through Earth's atmosphere over northwest Queensland, Australia, on May 20, 2023, accompanied by a raucous round of sonic booms. And U.S. government space-based sensors caught the fall.

Researchers later determined that the object underwent catastrophic fragmentation, producing one of the 20 most energetic events reported by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (CNEOS) since 1988 and the most energetic seen over Australia. It was equivalent to the explosion of a 7.1-kiloton bomb.

"For many fireballs, U.S. Government detections reported through NASA's CNEOS database provide an important starting point by establishing that an event occurred and, in many cases, providing basic parameters such as location, time and estimated energy," explained Elizabeth Silber, a senior research and development physicist at the U.S. Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico.

"Civil and scientific observing systems can then add independent measurements that help refine and validate that initial characterization," said Silber.

CNEOS, which is based at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, is NASA's center for computing asteroid and comet orbits and their odds of striking Earth. CNEOS computes high-precision orbits for such objects in support of NASA's Planetary Defense Coordination Office.

"The Alaska event is an especially useful example, because it was not reported by U.S. Government sensors in the CNEOS database. In this case, the event was reconstructed almost entirely from civil and scientific observations," Silber told Space.com.

She said that the seismic and infrasound data constrained the trajectory and acoustic energy, the video provided independent optical information, and the weather radar detected material from the fireball falling to Earth.

"So, the real strength is that these systems provide different and complementary information," said Silber. "When a U.S. Government detection is available, civil data can independently validate it and add much more detail. When one is not available, as in this case [for Alaska], the civil networks can still provide a surprisingly complete reconstruction."

The Alaska study shows how valuable it is to put together diverse types of observations once an event has occurred, said Silber. Each measurement responds to a different part of the event.

"Seismic and infrasound sensors record the atmospheric shock waves and can constrain the trajectory, fragmentation and energy," she added. "Optical observations provide an independent view of the luminous flight. Doppler weather radar can detect surviving material after it has slowed and entered dark flight."

Bottom line: no single sensor tells you everything.

"Combining independent observations lets us move from simply knowing that an event occurred to determining how the object traveled through the atmosphere, where it fragmented, how much energy it released, and whether material may have survived to the ground," said Silber.

Researchers got pretty lucky with the April 1, 2026 event over the South Atlantic, according to NASA's Rob Landis, a planetary defense specialist: Two civilian spacecraft located at different locations in geosynchronous orbit allowed them to conduct a rather unique investigation of this bolide.

"With two civilian resources, we can actually discuss things more openly," Landis, who's now a visiting vehicle integration manager for the International Space Station at NASA's Johnson Space Center, told Space.com.

Lightning-watching instruments not designed for detecting bolides, he said, "afford the science community to discuss these events and these sensors in a forthright, open manner. These lightning imagers give us opportunistic bonus science for those who study the 'hard rain.'"

Landis said that, in his personal view, there's a lot of smaller stuff getting through the atmosphere.

"To the casual observer, these certainly produce wonderful natural fireworks and are mostly harmless," Landis said. But, he stressed, it's important to be able to distinguish between natural events and human-made ones.

"It would be a horrific tragedy if any nation responded to a natural event — if they misinterpret it as a preemptive strike," cautioned Landis.

So, in the big picture, having collaborative, multiple and independent ways to observe atmospheric entries is of benefit to planetary defense thinkers.

"Planetary defense is not only about finding an object before it reaches Earth," Silber said. "It is also about understanding what happens during atmospheric entry — that is, how the object fragments, where it deposits its energy, how accurately we can reconstruct its trajectory and whether material survives to the ground."

Incoming events provide "real-world tests" of the methods and models used to answer those questions, said Silber.

Harkening back to the recent Alaska fireball fall, Silber said, was particularly valuable because it was unpredicted, yet the dense ground-based network allowed the trajectory and energetics to be reconstructed in considerable detail.

"From a planetary-defense perspective, that kind of redundancy is extremely useful. Space-based observations, seismic and infrasound networks, optical cameras, and weather radar each provide different information, and each has its own limitations," Silber said.

When several observation techniques are available, researchers can cross-check one another and produce a much more complete characterization of an event.

"That improves post-event situational awareness, helps validate physical models and strengthens our ability to interpret future atmospheric entries, whether they involve natural objects or artificial reentries," Silber concluded.

#608. American Airlines hikes annual fees on rewards cards for first time since 2018

American Airlines is raising the annual fee for two of its rewards credit cards for the first time since 2018 and adding new benefits like a TSA PreCheck credit and points from spending on hotels.

The fee on the Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard will go up to $150 a year from $99. That is the first hike since 2018, when it raised the fee from $95 to $99, an airline spokeswoman said.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Mastercard will also have a fee increase and will now cost $150 a year.

Airlines and their bank partners have been steadily raising fees on rewards credit cards.

Those cards generate billions of dollars a year for airlines, which make money when miles are sold to banks, which then give them to customers. American's move, announced Tuesday, follows similar increases by rivals such as United Airlines.

Meanwhile, American Express last year raised the fee on its popular Platinum card, which comes with airport lounge access, to $895 a year from $695. JPMorgan Chase increased the annual fee on its competing card, the Sapphire Reserve, to $795 from $550.

The new perks for the American card include three times AAdvantage miles earnings on hotels booked through American's portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit on in-flight purchases like food.

#606. Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk have completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk outside the International Space Station, marking another important step in a major upgrade to the orbiting laboratory's power system. The astronauts finished their work at 3:08 p.m. EDT.

During the spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's 2A electrical power channel. This is the seventh such array added to the station, providing additional electricity for essential operations, including the station's eventual safe and controlled deorbit.

Final Spacewalk Will Complete Solar Array Upgrade

The astronauts also performed several preliminary tasks to prepare for another spacewalk scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 5. During that mission, astronauts will install the eighth and final solar array on the station's 3B power channel. NASA plans to begin live coverage at 6:45 a.m., with information on how to watch available through the agency.

Once the final array is installed, the International Space Station's solar power expansion will be complete. Together, the eight new arrays will increase the station's available power by as much as 30%, raising its electricity generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts.

The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first. It was also the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the assembly, maintenance, and improvement of the International Space Station.

Nintendo's sci-fi shooter franchise is in dire straits, but we've got the solution to Samus's problems.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Metroid Prime 4: Beyond was, unfortunately, not the return many were hoping for when it finally arrived on Nintendo Switch consoles in 2025. After five years in development at Retro Studios, the original makers of the Metroid Prime series, fans were greeted with annoying side characters, a bike for Samus to roam the barren landscape on, and a deeply unsatisfying ending.

It’s a shame, considering how beloved the Metroid Prime series has been since the first title’s 2002 debut for the Nintendo GameCube. Many franchises were jumping from 2D to 3D at the turn of the millennium, and there were plenty of failures — but Metroid wasn’t one of them. The two sequels would enhance how players control Samus with powerful weapons and a multiplayer mode, but the 18-year gap between Metroid Prime 3 and 4 left players expecting something special.

Metroid Prime 4: Beyond’s average reception left fans wondering where the series can go next. It’s admittedly strange that Metroid Prime 2 and 3 have yet to debut on Nintendo Switch, either through the Nintendo Online service or as remasters.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has just dropped for Switch 2, and seeing Nintendo leverage one of the best games of all time for a modern take has given us an idea: let's give the Metroid Prime trilogy the remake treatment, taking inspiration from Capcom’s efforts with Resident Evil.

From 2002’s Resident Evil remake to the more recent successes with Resident Evil 2 & 4, Capcom has managed to recreate the feeling and survival horror tropes of the originals while modernizing the gameplay.

Whether it's the constant tension of being stalked by a Terminator-like Mr. X in 2019’s Resident Evil 2, or the palpable paranoia you feel exploring in Resident Evil 4 — the skin might be new, but the bones are undeniably "Resi."

Even recently-announced Resident Evil: Veronica — whilst a remake of 1999’s Code: Veronica — looks set to be a brand new take that evokes the feeling of the original game, but brings it into the modern era.

Prime 4 felt like a game out of time. Sure, it looked the part, but it felt decidedly like a GameCube game. So why not take a leaf out of Capcom's book, apply their "recapturing the vibes" mindset for a Metroid Prime Trilogy Remake, using the Prime 4 engine as its foundation.

2023’s Metroid Prime Remastered showed off the venerable title with better textures and widescreen support, but a remake powered by the fourth game’s engine could showcase the opening and Tallon IV in a whole new light.

Similar to 2002’s Resident Evil Remake with the Spencer Mansion, places would feel familiar but fresh, thanks to updated graphics, better sound, and support for HD Rumble 2 that could help the player become more immersed in the game. And of course, you can change a few things to play off people's expectations.

If Nintendo is feeling brave, the reimagining could even begin at the end of Zero Mission, which is set just before Metroid Prime. Controlling Samus with all her abilities, facing off against Mother Brain in an area not seen in 3D, could be a great introduction to old and new players, as well as giving the opportunity to remake an area from a previous title. Then, players could escape to Samus’ ship, with the ability to pilot it to the Orpheron ship, where Prime begins.

A remake (or remakes) would obviously mean a big step-up in graphics and gameplay across all three games, but it could also herald the long-awaited return of its multiplayer mode from Metroid Prime 2, something that Metroid Prime 4: Beyond bizarrely left out.

Up to four players could take part in one of two modes here - Deathmatch and Bounty Mode, which had players compete against one another by collecting coins to win matches. There were four arenas to choose from, with an additional two to unlock when players got far enough in Prime 2’s single-player mode.

It was a fun time, and its absence in Prime 4: Beyond felt like a big miss, especially with the prospect of playing this mode online with others and using the Switch 2 features like Game Chat.

A remake could fix this injustice, and even expand on the concept by offering new multiplayer modes alongside maps based on locations from across the Prime series. You could even add a co-op mode for the campaign, and a horde mode for co-op fans to enjoy online too.

As it stands in 2026, the Metroid series feels adrift once more. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond will be lost to the sands of time, a mediocre entry in a series filled with bangers. As the latest Nintendo Direct eagerly showcased Donkey Kong, Zelda, and plenty of third-party releases, Samus was notably absent. Sure, she's just had a game, but it's hard not to be nervous after the drought that Metroid players had to suffer in the 2010s.

Capcom was in a similar lull after 2012’s disappointing Resident Evil 6, a bloated and confusing entry that made players fear the end of the series. But the seventh entry, alongside the Resident Evil 2 Remake in 2019, breathed new life into the franchise, which has proved as tough to kill as any of Umbrella's bioweapons.

Metroid's fate feels equally in the balance right now, and in a world where game studios are closing down and rivals like Microsoft are shrinking their focus to big-hitter franchises, Nintendo could easily let Metroid fall back into obscurity. Refocusing on what makes the series iconic is the key to its success, and modern remakes of the originals might just be what they need to rediscover that Metroid magic.

There are some easy wins out there to keep fans engaged; it’d still be great to see more games appear on the Nintendo Online service, like Metroid Prime 2, and we'd love more 2D entries after the excellent Metroid Dread, but nothing hits like Prime, and Prime isn't hitting right now.

If not, then I fear Samus will be riding her Vi-O-La into the sunset, deep within the barren wasteland of Sol Valley for the foreseeable future.

Liftoff occurred today (Nov. 2) at 11:41 a.m. ET.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rocket Lab launched its 99th mission to date today (Nov. 2), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite toward orbit.

An Electron rocket lifted off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site today at 11:41 a.m. EST (1641 GMT; 5:41 a.m. on Nov. 3 local New Zealand time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Sea God Surveys," is carrying an Earth-observing radar satellite to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Japanese company iQPS. All went according to plan: The spacecraft was deployed at an altitude of 357 miles (575 kilometers), Rocket Lab announced about 56 minutes after launch.

"The Sea God Surveys" was Rocket Lab's 10th launch to date for iQPS, which is assembling a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO.

SAR satellites offer advantages over those that view our planet in optical wavelengths. They can peer through cloud cover, for example, and study our planet at night as well as during the day.

Today's launch was the 99th overall for Rocket Lab and the 90th for the two-stage, 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron, which gives small satellites dedicated rides to space. The workhorse vehicle has now flown 17 times this year.

Rocket Lab's other nine launches to date have been conducted by HASTE, a suborbital version of Electron that allows customers to test their tech in the hypersonic flight environment. HASTE (short for "Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron") debuted in June 2023 and generally flies classified payloads.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11:55 a.m. ET on Nov. 2 with news of successful launch, then again at 1 p.m. EST with news of successful satellite deployment.

#603. Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang

New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.

Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.

What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.

"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.

"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.

Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.

"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."

How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe

RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.

Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.

The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.

Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.

One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.

Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.

If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.

Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.

"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."

For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.

Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.

These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.

Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.

The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.

Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?

After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.

Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.

These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?

Scientists needed a more definitive sign.

"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.

To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.

An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.

"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.

The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.

"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."

Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.

Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression

To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.

"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.

"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."

Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.

"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."

The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).

The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.

Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.

Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.

Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies

Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.

That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.

The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.

However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.

"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."

While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.

By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.

"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.

New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter

Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.

During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.

These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.

Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.

The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.

The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Starshield has been in the news a fair bit recently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

SpaceX is building and operating two satellite networks at the moment, Starlink and Starshield. What’s the difference between the two, and who uses them?

For more than a week in October 2026, Ukrainian drone operators found their high-speed satellite links shut off. Officials in Kyiv said that terminals for SpaceX’s Starshield network stopped working at speeds of above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) from Oct. 14, hampering efforts to conduct defensive operations and intercept Russian drones. Full connectivity was restored on Oct. 24, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The arguments over who did what continue, but the affair highlighted how little is publicly understood about Starshield — what it is, how it relates to Starlink, and how it is operated.

Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial, mass-market satellite internet service. The company says it now has more than 11,000 Starlink broadband and mobile satellites in orbit, operating approximately 342 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. This follows years of deployment using the company's Falcon 9 rocket..

The network serves consumers, enterprises and government customers across more than 160 countries. It is owned and operated by SpaceX. Anyone from a rural household to an airline can buy a terminal and a service plan.

Governments are also customers, with public agencies using Starlink for a range of purposes including connectivity, disaster response and national security, notably in the case of Ukraine in the wake of the invasion by Russia, which began in February 2022 and is ongoing.

Starshield is SpaceX’s network for serving national security customers. The company announced the program in December 2022, stating it would apply Starlink technology and SpaceX's launch capability to government needs, initially in three areas: Earth observation, communications and hosted payloads.

"They are using the same satellite buses," says Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. “They look the same, but they have a lot more kit on them that allows them to do more things. They provide similar broadband internet, but with more secure hardware and software and hardened systems.”

The company says it has won multi-billion-dollar, multiyear contracts from the U.S. military in 2026 for Starshield-related services.

Some Starshield satellites may also carry sensors for intelligence and surveillance. But much about Starshield is secretive, with its finances not revealed and launches often classified.

Starshield is made up of a range of different assets, including spy satellites, military data satellites, and secure communications for ground users.

The spy satellites are sent into orbit in launches for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), for a "proliferated architecture" of spy satellites, including electro-optical, radar and relay spacecraft. The NRO does not use the Starshield name, but said earlier this year that it had launched more than 200 satellites in recent years, many of which are for its proliferated architecture.

Then there is the Space Data Network Backbone. The U.S. Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion fixed-price contract to build the network, previously known as MILNET, using Starshield satellites. It is meant to move data quickly between missile-warning sensors and interceptors as part of the Trump administration's Golden Dome missile defense plan. A prototype is due by the end of 2027. A Space Force official has described MILNET as government-owned and operated by SpaceX as a contractor, under Space Force oversight.

Starshield provides encrypted connectivity for military users through terminals. These can be dedicated Starshield terminals, or Starlink terminals for Starshield services.

Crucially, the networks overlap. "Those Starshield satellites are physically separate from Starlink satellites, but the Starshield satellites can use the Starlink network if they need to," Bowen said. That interoperability is available to U.S. national security users, he added, "but not if you're a commercial user of Starlink."

Use restrictions differ, too. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said that Starlink's terms of service bar its use for offensive drone strikes, while decisions about Starshield use rest with the U.S. government.

Who controls Starshield is a question that entered the public consciousness in the wake of the Ukraine Starshield speed limit affair. The U.S. government is the customer, and also in some cases the owner, but SpaceX builds the satellites, operates the underlying Starlink network on which some Starshield services run and, in some arrangements, operates the Starshield satellites themselves. How this command is divided between the government and SpaceX is unclear.

Bowen compared it to the U.K.’s Skynet military satellite system, in which contractor Babcock operates the satellites. "The actual button punching is done by the contractors, but the military and government are in the room and are calling the shots,” he said.

That question matters, because it determines whether SpaceX can act on its own or only with government oversight and approval.

Starshield appears set to become more central to U.S. military space. The Space Data Network Backbone prototype is expected next year, while NRO launches will continue, according to contracts. With SpaceX now a public company, quarterly reports could provide more insight into the system. For now, however, much remains classified.

#600. Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule

Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.

Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor

Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.

The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.

Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.

A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips

The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.

At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.

When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.

This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.

How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin

The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.

The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.

But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.

Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect

To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.

Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.

The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.

"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.

The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.

International Collaboration Solves the Mystery

The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.

Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.

This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.

"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.

The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.

Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.

"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.

The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).

Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

#598. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

White Vision, Hex Vision, and Ultron all converge in this spirited new superhero series.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Marvel Studios' existential superhero series "VisionQuest" has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers.

The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's "WandaVision" and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps.

And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest.

Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned!

We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is.

Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods.

*This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest.

We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger.

From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision.

One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision.

So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one.

So, the Vision we see in "VisionQuest" is the physical body of White Vision, injected with thoughts and remembrances of the model that was magically resurrected by Wanda. Confused yet? Don't worry, it's going to get weirder.

In addition to the two versions of Vision from "WandaVision," numerous other AIs exist within Vision's skull and are all represented by human avatars acting as factions of his ravaged psyche.

Cast your mind all the way back to 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and you'll remember that Vision was conceived from a combination of the artificial brain of Ultron, the Mind Stone, and fragments of Tony Stark’s AI butler companion, J.A.R.V.I.S., who was named after the real Jarvis seen in the "Agent Carter" TV series.

J.A.R.V.I.S. appears in "VisionQuest" as his own unique entity, alongside another of Tony Stark's AI helpers, E.D.I.T.H., aka the AI in the smart glasses that Stark left to Peter Parker after his death. She shows up in "Spider-Man: Far From Home," which is a great movie but not an essential viewing if you're preparing for "VisionQuest."

Then let's toss in the fact that papa Ultron (James Spader) is buzzing around in Vision’s cranium, creating what’s been described as more or less an "Age of Ultron" and a "WandaVision" sequel at the same time. As it turns out, Vision did not destroy Ultron at the end of "Age of Ultron"; he copied his code and absorbed him, so now the rabid robot lives on in Vision’s brain.

The show’s narrative is centered around the complicated relationship between Vision and his son Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Tommy was created by Wanda's Hex and should have disappeared when it collapsed, but both he and his brother Billy survived through magical shenanigans that are explained in 2024's "Agatha All Along."

Those two Maximoff boys, Tommy and Billy, both vanished from existence at the conclusion of "WandaVision." "Agatha All Along" exposed the truth that their consciousnesses entered the ether before expiring, only to reemerge into the souls of two teenage boys who had just perished, therefore returning them to life. Are you still with us? Good, just checking.

The finale of "Agatha All Along" hinted at the return of the estranged Tommy, and "VisionQuest" dives into that dangling plot point with relish!

Every show needs an antagonist, and the voices in Vision's head can't do all the work. "VisionQuest" has introduced a duo of villains for Vision to contend with. Neither of them has shown up in the MCU previously, though, so you don't need to do any research here.

With a massive bounty on his head after breaking free from S.W.O.R.D.'s control, White Vision must contend with a new villainous foe in the form of a mysterious mercenary named Paladin (Todd Stashwick).

This enigmatic Marvel Comics character was created by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino and was first seen prowling the pages of "Daredevil #150" back in 1978. He's basically a gun-for-hire in the Marvel universe, often hired to fight alongside or against various heroes depending on the story. We don't know much about his motivations in the show, but we'll learn more as it goes on.

"VisionQuest" also shines a spotlight on the bizarro character of Ultron's "bride," Jocasta, though the MCU version of this character diverges wildly from the comic book inspiration.

It's enough to drive one to madness! Between all the father-son dynamics dancing around the eight scheduled episodes, being hunted down by mercs, and his transcendent search for meaning, Vision and his saga are hopefully headed to a peaceful end.

Created by Terry Matalas ("Star Trek: Picard," "12 Monkeys") and airing two new chapters each Tuesday night on Disney+, VisionQuest is bolstered by a cast that includes Ruaridh Mollica, T'Nia Miller, Lauren Morais, Orla Brady, Diane Morgan, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy.
